Infiltration Rates at Several Field Sites
When rain falls faster than soil can absorb it, the excess water becomes surface runoff. The maximum rate at which a soil can absorb water, measured in millimeters per hour (mm/hr), is called its infiltration capacity, and it varies based on soil texture, compaction, and vegetation. Soil scientist Declan Murphy claims that during a moderately intense rainstorm delivering precipitation at 45 mm/hr, runoff would likely occur at most, but not all, of the field sites listed in the table.
prompt: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Murphy's claim?

choices.A: Only Meadowbrook has an organic matter content below 4%.
choices.B: Only Clearwater has a slope greater than 7 degrees.
choices.C: Only Pinegrove has an infiltration capacity greater than 45 mm/hr.
choices.D: Only Riverbend has an organic matter content greater than 5%.

explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. Murphy claims that a rainstorm at 45 mm/hr would cause runoff at most, but not all, of the field sites. Runoff occurs when rainfall exceeds a soil's infiltration capacity, so the claim requires that most sites have infiltration capacities below 45 mm/hr while at least one does not. The table shows Meadowbrook (22 mm/hr), Riverbend (38 mm/hr), and Clearwater (29 mm/hr) all fall below 45 mm/hr, while only Pinegrove (51 mm/hr) exceeds it. Thus runoff would occur at three of the four sites — most, but not all — directly supporting Murphy's claim.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect. Although it accurately describes the table — Riverbend (5.8%) is the only site with organic matter content greater than 5% — this information is irrelevant to Murphy's claim. The claim is about whether rainfall at 45 mm/hr would produce runoff, which depends on infiltration capacity, not organic matter content.
